title: The Tiamat pile: five dragons against a telegraphed board wipe

board.you: Turn 8, Tiamat just resolved (cast, so the search trigger is on the stack). Battlefield: Tiamat, Temur Ascendancy, Garruk's Uprising, six lands. Life 31.
board.table: Player 2 (the known sweeper deck — Esper) has SEVEN lands untapped after passing with mana up two turns running; everyone at the table reads Supreme-Verdict-shaped mana. Player 3 and 4 have small boards and are visibly waiting for Player 2 to act.

scenario.question: Tiamat's trigger searches for up to five differently-named Dragon cards to HAND — the pile is yours to design. Against telegraphed sweeper mana: do you fetch the all-gas pile (Terror of the Peaks, Scourge of Valkas, Lathliss, Miirym, Atarka) and commit next turn, fetch a resilience pile built around haste + protection pieces you can deploy across two turns, or fetch value-recursion (Haven of the Spirit Dragon is on-board fetchable? — no, it's a land — design around what the deck actually offers: which five names, and why)? Name the exact five cards and the sequencing plan.

branches.choice: All-gas pile — Terror of the Peaks, Scourge of Valkas, Lathliss, Miirym, Atarka — and commit next turn
branches.line: Fetch the five biggest payoffs. Next turn: deploy as many as seven lands allow — with eminence that is Terror ({2}{R}{R}) plus Scourge of Valkas ({1}{R}{R}{R}), both hasty via Temur Ascendancy — and attack, holding the rest for the turn after.
branches.signals: The table watched Tiamat fetch five and watched you slam two payoffs into seven untapped Esper lands. Player 2 does not need to read tells; the Verdict timing is now scripted for them.
branches.coalition_risk: Maximal. You become the archenemy on the exact turn the sweeper deck is best positioned, and Players 3 and 4 — visibly waiting for Player 2 to act — will happily let the wrath resolve.
branches.coaching: The math fails before the politics do. Six lands plus a drop means roughly two Dragons per turn even with eminence — you cannot deploy enough of this pile to kill Player 2 through seven mana of held interaction before the sweep, so the wrath eats Tiamat plus your two best payoffs while three uncastable dragons watch from your hand. This is the textbook wrath-math violation (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math): commit exactly what wins before the wrath, and nothing here wins before it. The all-gas pile is the right fetch at a tapped-out table; it is the wrong fetch into telegraphed mana.

branches.choice: Staggered pile — Hellkite Courser, Goldspan Dragon, Miirym, Lathliss, Terror of the Peaks — played in two waves
branches.line: Fetch pieces that either ignore the sweeper or rebuild through it. Wave one (next turn): Goldspan Dragon ({2}{R}{R} after eminence), attack Player 2 with Goldspan and Tiamat — both hasty via Ascendancy — pressuring the Esper life total and forcing the Verdict onto a two-body board; the attack banks a Treasure that survives the wipe. Wave two (post-wrath): Hellkite Courser ({3}{R}{R} after eminence) puts The Ur-Dragon onto the battlefield from the command zone with haste; attack with both, the commander trigger draws two and deploys Miirym free from hand, then the commander returns to the command zone at end step — untouchable, untaxed, having never been cast. Then Lathliss and Terror unload into the Miirym doubler.
branches.signals: Wave one reads as pressure, not commitment — two attackers against a control deck is what the whole table wants from you. The scary names stay hidden in hand where the sweeper cannot price them.
branches.coalition_risk: Medium and managed. You take the archenemy mantle only after the table's one near-certain reset has been spent, and the Courser turn ends with the commander safely back in the zone.
branches.coaching: The point of designing a Tiamat pile into sweeper mana is fetching cards the sweeper cannot tax: Treasures are artifacts, your draw-and-haste layer (Temur Ascendancy, Garruk's Uprising) is enchantments, and a Courser-loaned commander is a rental — even if Player 2 wipes in response to the Courser trigger, the commander goes to the graveyard and the state-based action returns him to the command zone, and no tax accrues because the tax counts only casts from the command zone, which this never was. You lose Tiamat and Goldspan to the wipe; that is the price of forcing it on a board you chose. Goldfish note: protection is in hand by turn 6 in 66.4% of games — if you are actually holding Teferi's Protection or Heroic Intervention here, you can shift weight toward Branch A's speed. Design the pile for the third of games you are not.

citations.quote: If a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone.
A commander cast from the command zone costs an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game.

branches.choice: Fetch gas but deploy nothing until the sweeper resolves
branches.line: Fetch any five (the Branch B names are fine), then pass with mana up for turns, deploying zero Dragons until Player 2 is forced to spend the wrath on Players 3 and 4 — or until they tap out for something else.
branches.signals: Total passivity from the Dragon deck after a five-card Tiamat fetch fools nobody — the table knows your hand is loaded, and Player 2 knows the Verdict is live against you whenever you finally move.
branches.coalition_risk: Low now, worst-case later: Players 3 and 4 have small boards, so Player 2 may simply never be forced to sweep — and every stand-off turn their seven lands also fund counters and draw while your three free draw steps rotate to all three opponents.
branches.coaching: The stand-off math runs against you. Tiamat dies to the sweep whenever it comes, board or no board, so holding back protects almost nothing you have not already committed — while Branch B's Goldspan probe pressures the Esper life total and banks sweep-proof Treasure at the cost of one fetched card. Passive turns are free draw steps for the table (strategy:pivot-point), and against a draw-go deck specifically, time is their axis, not yours. Force the wrath on a board you designed to lose cheaply; do not wait for a tap-out that a competent control player will never volunteer.

recommendation.choice: Staggered pile — Hellkite Courser, Goldspan Dragon, Miirym, Lathliss, Terror of the Peaks — played in two waves
recommendation.rationale: Into seven lands of telegraphed Verdict mana, the winning pile is the one that makes the sweeper hit air: force the wipe with a cheap two-attacker probe, keep the multipliers in hand, then rent the commander through Hellkite Courser for a draw-two-plus-free-Miirym turn that ends with him back in the command zone, untaxed (903.8's tax counts casts, and 903.9a covers him even if he dies mid-loan). Your enchantment layer survives the wrath, so wave two arrives hasty and drawing — the reset becomes your pivot point (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math, strategy:pivot-point). Branch A commits into the wrath's best turn; Branch C waits for a tap-out that never comes.
